{{Short description|Special triangle in geometry}}
[[File:Calabi triangle.svg|300px|right|thumb|A Calabi triangle is a triangle <math> ABC </math> with three squares, each of which is described as the green region and blue vertices and edges]]

The '''Calabi triangle''' is a special [[triangle]] found by [[Eugenio Calabi]]. 

It is the unique triangle that has 3 different placements for the largest [[square]] that it contains, and is not the [[equilateral triangle]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Calabi |first=Eugenio |author-link=Eugenio Calabi |date=3 Nov 1997 |title=Outline of Proof Regarding Squares Wedged in Triangle |url=http://www.people.fas.harvard.edu/~sfinch/csolve/calabi.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20121212215151/http://www.people.fas.harvard.edu/~sfinch/csolve/calabi.html |archive-date=12 December 2012 |access-date=3 May 2018}}</ref> It is an [[isosceles]] triangle which is [[obtuse triangle|obtuse]] with an [[irrational number|irrational]] but [[algebraic number|algebraic]] ratio between the lengths of its sides and its base.{{sfn|Stewart|2004|p=15}}<ref>{{cite book |last1=Conway |first1=J.H. |author-link1=John Horton Conway |title=The Book of Numbers |last2=Guy |first2=R.K. |author-link2=Richard K. Guy |publisher=Springer-Verlag |year=1996 |location=New York |page=206 |contribution=Calabi's Triangle |contribution-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0--3rcO7dMYC&pg=PA206}}</ref><ref name="Wolfram">{{mathworld|title=Calabi's Triangle|id=CalabisTriangle}}</ref>

Consider the largest square that can be placed in an arbitrary triangle. It may be that such a square could be positioned in the triangle in more than one way. In the [[equilateral triangle]], the largest such square can be positioned in three different ways. Calabi found that there is exactly one other case, and so it is named the Calabi triangle.

==Shape==
The triangle {{math|△''ABC''}} is [[isosceles]] which has the same length of sides as {{math|''AB'' {{=}} ''AC''}}. If the ratio of the base to either leg is {{mvar|x}}, we can set that {{math|''AB'' {{=}} ''AC'' {{=}} 1, ''BC'' {{=}} {{mvar|x}}}}. Then we can consider the following three cases:
;case 1) {{math|△''ABC''}} is [[acute triangle]]:
:The condition is <math>0 < x < \sqrt{2}</math>.
:In this case {{math|{{mvar|x}} {{=}} 1}} is valid for [[equilateral triangle]].
;case 2) {{math|△''ABC''}} is [[right triangle]]:
:The condition is <math>x = \sqrt{2}</math>.
:In this case no value is valid.
;case 3) {{math|△''ABC''}} is [[obtuse triangle]]:
:The condition is <math>\sqrt{2} < x < 2</math>.
:In this case the Calabi triangle is valid for the largest positive root of <math> 2x^3 - 2x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0</math> at <math>x = 1.55138752454832039226...</math> ({{oeis|A046095}}).

{{Hidden begin|title = Example of answer|titlestyle = text-align:center;}}
[[File:Example_figure_of_Calabi_triangle_01.svg|right|220px|Example figure of Calabi triangle 01]]

Consider the case of {{math|''AB'' {{=}} ''AC'' {{=}} 1, ''BC'' {{=}} {{mvar|x}}}}. Then
:<math>0 < x < 2.</math>
Let a base angle be {{mvar|θ}} and a square be {{math|□''DEFG''}} on base {{math|''BC''}} with its side length as {{mvar|a}}.
Let {{mvar|H}} be the foot of the perpendicular drawn from the apex {{mvar|A}} to the base. Then
:<math>\begin{align}
HB &= HC = \cos\theta = \frac{x}{2}, \\
AH &= \sin\theta = \frac{x}{2}\tan\theta , \\
0 &< \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}.
\end{align}</math>
Then {{math|''HB'' {{=}} {{sfrac|{{mvar|x}}|2}}}} and {{math|''HE'' {{=}} {{sfrac|{{mvar|a}}|2}}}}, so {{math|''EB'' {{=}} {{sfrac|{{mvar|x}} - {{mvar|a}}|2}}}}.

From △DEB ∽ △AHB,
:<math>\begin{align}
& EB : DE = HB : AH \\
&\Leftrightarrow \bigg(\frac{x - a}{2}\bigg) : a = \cos \theta : \sin \theta = 1 : \tan \theta \\
&\Leftrightarrow a = \bigg(\frac{x - a}{2}\bigg)\tan \theta \\
&\Leftrightarrow a = \frac{x \tan \theta}{\tan \theta + 2}. \\
\end{align}</math>

=== case 1) {{math|△''ABC''}} is acute triangle ===
[[File:Example_figure_of_Calabi_triangle_02.svg|right|220px|Example figure of Calabi triangle 02]]

Let {{math|□''IJKL''}} be a square on side {{math|''AC''}} with its side length as {{mvar|b}}.
From △ABC ∽ △IBJ,
:<math>\begin{align}
& AB : IJ = BC : BJ \\
&\Leftrightarrow 1 : b = x : BJ \\
&\Leftrightarrow BJ = bx.
\end{align}</math>

From △JKC ∽ △AHC,
:<math>\begin{align}
& JK : JC = AH : AC \\
&\Leftrightarrow b : JC = \frac{x}{2}\tan\theta : 1 \\
&\Leftrightarrow JC = \frac{2b}{x\tan\theta}.
\end{align}</math>

Then 
:<math>\begin{align}
&x = BC = BJ + JC = bx + \frac{2b}{x\tan\theta} \\
&\Leftrightarrow x = b\frac{x^2 \tan\theta + 2}{x\tan\theta} \\
&\Leftrightarrow b = \frac{x^2 \tan\theta}{x^2 \tan\theta + 2}.
\end{align}</math>

Therefore, if two squares are congruent,
:<math>\begin{align}
&a = b \\
&\Leftrightarrow \frac{x \tan \theta}{\tan \theta + 2} = \frac{x^2 \tan\theta}{x^2 \tan\theta + 2} \\
&\Leftrightarrow x\tan\theta\cdot(x^2 \tan\theta + 2) = x^2 \tan\theta(\tan\theta + 2) \\
&\Leftrightarrow x\tan\theta\cdot(x(\tan\theta + 2) - (x^2 \tan\theta + 2)) = 0 \\
&\Leftrightarrow x\tan\theta\cdot(x\tan\theta - 2)\cdot(x - 1) = 0 \\
&\Leftrightarrow 2\sin\theta\cdot2(\sin\theta - 1)\cdot(x - 1) = 0.
\end{align}</math>

In this case, <math>\frac{\pi}{4} < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}, 2\sin\theta\cdot2(\sin\theta - 1) \ne 0.</math>

Therefore <math>x = 1</math>, it means that {{math|△''ABC''}} is equilateral triangle.

=== case 2) {{math|△''ABC''}} is right triangle ===
[[File:Example_figure_of_Calabi_triangle_03.svg|right|400px|Example figure of Calabi triangle 03]]

In this case, <math>x = \sqrt{2}, \tan\theta = 1</math>, so <math>a = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}, b = \frac{1}{2}.</math>

Then no value is valid.
{{Clear}}

=== case 3) {{math|△''ABC''}} is obtuse triangle ===
[[File:Example_figure_of_Calabi_triangle_04.svg|right|475px|Example figure of Calabi triangle 04]]

Let {{math|□''IJKA''}} be a square on base {{math|''AC''}} with its side length as {{mvar|b}}.

From △AHC ∽ △JKC,
:<math>\begin{align}
& AH : HC = JK : KC \\
&\Leftrightarrow \sin\theta : \cos\theta = b : (1-b) \\
&\Leftrightarrow b\cos\theta = (1-b)\sin\theta \\
&\Leftrightarrow b = (1-b)\tan\theta \\
&\Leftrightarrow b = \frac{\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}.
\end{align}</math>

Therefore, if two squares are congruent,
:<math>\begin{align}
&a = b \\
&\Leftrightarrow \frac{x \tan \theta}{\tan \theta + 2} = \frac{\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta} \\
&\Leftrightarrow \frac{x}{\tan \theta + 2} = \frac{1}{1+\tan\theta} \\
&\Leftrightarrow x(\tan\theta + 1) = \tan\theta + 2 \\
&\Leftrightarrow (x - 1)\tan\theta = 2 - x.
\end{align}</math>

In this case,
:<math>\tan\theta = \frac{AH}{CH} = \frac{\sqrt{AC^2 - CH^2}}{CH} = \frac{\sqrt{1 - \left( \frac{x}{2} \right)^2}}{\frac{x}{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{(2+x)(2-x)}}{x}.</math>

So, we can input the value of {{math|tan''θ''}},
:<math>\begin{align}
&(x - 1)\tan\theta = 2 - x \\
&\Leftrightarrow (x - 1)\frac{\sqrt{(2 + x)(2 - x)}}{x} = 2 - x \\
&\Leftrightarrow (2 - x)\cdot((x - 1)^2 (2 + x) - x^2 (2 - x)) = 0 \\
&\Leftrightarrow (2 - x)\cdot(2x^3 - 2x^2 - 3x + 2) = 0.
\end{align}</math>

In this case, <math>\sqrt{2} < x < 2</math>, we can get the following equation:
:<math>2x^3 - 2x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0.</math>

{{Hidden end}}

== Root of Calabi's equation ==
If {{mvar|x}} is the largest positive [[zero of a function|root]] of Calabi's equation:
: <math> 2x^3 - 2x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0 , \sqrt{2} < x < 2</math>
we can calculate the value of {{mvar|x}} by following methods.

=== Newton's method ===
We can set the function <math>f : \mathbb{R} \rarr \mathbb{R}</math> as follows:
: <math>\begin{align}
f(x) &= 2x^3 - 2x^2 -3x + 2, \\
f'(x)&= 6x^2 - 4x - 3 = 6\bigg(x - \frac{1}{3}\bigg)^2 - \frac{11}{3}.
\end{align}</math>
The function {{mvar|f}} is [[Continuous function|continuous]] and [[Differentiable function|differentiable]] on <math>\mathbb{R}</math> and
: <math>\begin{align}
f(\sqrt{2}) &= \sqrt{2} - 2 < 0, \\
f(2)        &= 4 > 0, \\
f'(x)       &> 0 , \forall x \in [\sqrt{2}, 2].
\end{align}</math>
Then {{mvar|f}} is [[Monotonic function|monotonically increasing function]] and by [[Intermediate value theorem]], the Calabi's equation {{math|{{mvar|f}}({{mvar|x}}) {{=}} 0}} has unique solution in open interval <math>\sqrt{2} < x < 2</math>.

The value of {{mvar|x}} is calculated by [[Newton's method]] as follows:
: <math>\begin{align}
x_0 &= \sqrt{2}, \\
x_{n+1} &= x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)} = \frac{4x_n^3-2x_n^2-2}{6x_n^2-4x_n-3}.
\end{align}</math>

=== Cardano's method ===
The value of {{mvar|x}} can expressed with [[complex number]]s by using [[Cardano's method]]:
: <math> x = {1 \over 3} \Bigg(1 + \sqrt[3]{-23 + 3i \sqrt{237} \over 4} + \sqrt[3]{-23 - 3i \sqrt{237} \over 4} \Bigg) .</math><ref name="Wolfram" />{{sfn|Stewart|2004|pp=7-10}}{{efn|If we set the [[polar form]] of complex number, we can calculate the value of {{mvar|x}} as follows:
: <math>\begin{align}
\alpha           &= re^{i\varphi}=r(\cos\varphi +i\sin\varphi)=\frac{-23 + 3i \sqrt{237}}{4} , \\
r                &= \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{(-23)^2+9 \cdot 237} = \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{2 \cdot 11^3} = \Bigg(\sqrt{\frac{11}{2}}\Bigg)^3, \\
\cos\varphi      &= - \frac{23}{4}\frac{1}{r} = - \frac{23 \cdot 2 \sqrt{2}}{4 \cdot 11 \sqrt{11}} = - \frac{23}{11 \sqrt{22}}, \\
\sqrt[3]{\alpha} &= \sqrt[3]{r}e^{\frac{i\varphi}{3}}=\sqrt[3]{r}\Big(\cos\Big(\frac{\varphi}{3}\Big) +i\sin\Big(\frac{\varphi}{3}\Big)\Big), \\
\sqrt[3]{\alpha} + \sqrt[3]{\bar{\alpha}} &= 2 \sqrt[3]{r} \cos\Big(\frac{\varphi}{3}\Big) = \sqrt{22} \cos\!\bigg( {1 \over 3} \cos^{-1}\!\!\bigg(\!-{23 \over 11 \sqrt{22}} \bigg) \bigg), \\
x &= \frac{1}{3}\bigg(1 + \sqrt[3]{\alpha} + \sqrt[3]{\bar{\alpha}} \bigg) = {1 \over 3} \bigg(1 + \sqrt{22} \cos\!\bigg( {1 \over 3} \cos^{-1}\!\!\bigg(\!-{23 \over 11 \sqrt{22}} \bigg) \bigg) \bigg).
\end{align}</math>
Then this Cardano's method is equivalent as [[#Viète's method|Viète's method]].}}

=== Viète's method ===
The value of {{mvar|x}} can also be expressed without [[complex number]]s by using [[Cubic equation#Trigonometric solution for three real roots|Viète's method]]:
: <math>\begin{align}
x &= {1 \over 3} \bigg(1 + \sqrt{22} \cos\!\bigg( {1 \over 3} \cos^{-1}\!\!\bigg(\!-{23 \over 11 \sqrt{22}} \bigg) \bigg) \bigg) \\
  &=  1.55138752454832039226195251026462381516359170380389\cdots .
\end{align}</math>{{sfn|Stewart|2004|p=15}}

=== Lagrange's method ===
The value of {{mvar|x}} has [[continued fraction]] representation by [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange|Lagrange]]'s method as follows:<br />[1, 1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 2, 1, 5, 2, 1, 3, 1, 1, 390, ...] =<br />
:<math>1 + \cfrac{1}{1 + 
    \cfrac{1}{1 + 
    \cfrac{1}{4 + 
    \cfrac{1}{2 + 
    \cfrac{1}{1 + 
    \cfrac{1}{2 + 
    \cfrac{1}{1 + 
    \cfrac{1}{5 + 
    \cfrac{1}{2 + 
    \cfrac{1}{1 + 
    \cfrac{1}{3 + 
    \cfrac{1}{1 + 
    \cfrac{1}{1 + 
    \cfrac{1}{390 + \cdots    }}}}}}}}}}}}}}</math>.<ref name="Wolfram" /><ref>{{Citation|last=Joseph-Louis|first=Lagrange|author-link=Joseph-Louis Lagrange|year=1769|title=Sur la résolution des équations numériques|journal=Mémoires de l'Académie royale des Sciences et Belles-lettres de Berlin|volume=23|url=http://sites.mathdoc.fr/cgi-bin/oeitem?id=OE_LAGRANGE__2_539_0}} - [https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN308899857?tify=%7B%22pages%22%3A%5B544%2C545%5D%2C%22pan%22%3A%7B%22x%22%3A0.947%2C%22y%22%3A0.64%7D%2C%22view%22%3A%22toc%22%2C%22zoom%22%3A0.354%7D Œuvres II, p.539-578.]</ref><ref>{{Citation|last=Joseph-Louis|first=Lagrange|author-link=Joseph-Louis Lagrange|year=1770|title=Additions au mémoire sur la résolution des équations numériques|journal=Mémoires de l'Académie royale des Sciences et Belles-lettres de Berlin|volume=24|url=http://sites.mathdoc.fr/cgi-bin/oeitem?id=OE_LAGRANGE__2_581_0}} - [https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN308899857?tify=%7B%22pages%22%3A%5B586%2C587%5D%2C%22pan%22%3A%7B%22x%22%3A0.947%2C%22y%22%3A0.64%7D%2C%22view%22%3A%22toc%22%2C%22zoom%22%3A0.354%7D Œuvres II, p.581-652.]</ref>{{efn|text=If a [[continued fraction]] {{math|[''a''{{sub|0}}, ''a''{{sub|1}}, ''a''{{sub|2}}, ...]}} are found, with numerators {{mvar|h}}{{sub|1}}, {{mvar|h}}{{sub|2}}, ... and denominators {{mvar|k}}{{sub|1}}, {{mvar|k}}{{sub|2}}, ... then the relevant recursive relation is that of [[Gaussian bracket]]s:

:{{math|''h''{{sub|''n''}} {{=}} ''a''{{sub|''n''}}''h''{{sub|''n'' − 1}} + ''h''{{sub|''n'' − 2}}}},
:{{math|''k''{{sub|''n''}} {{=}} ''a''{{sub|''n''}}''k''{{sub|''n'' − 1}} + ''k''{{sub|''n'' − 2}}}}.

The successive convergents are given by the formula

:{{bigmath|{{sfrac|''h''{{sub|''n''}}|''k''{{sub|''n''}}}} {{=}} {{sfrac|''a''{{sub|''n''}}''h''{{sub|''n'' − 1}} + ''h''{{sub|''n'' − 2}}|''a''{{sub|''n''}}''k''{{sub|''n'' − 1}} + ''k''{{sub|''n'' − 2}}}}}}.

The rational approxmation of {{mvar|x}} is {{sfrac|{{mvar|h}}{{sub|95}}|{{mvar|k}}{{sub|95}}}} and an error bounds {{mvar|ε}} is as follows:
:<math>
\begin{align}
x &\approx \frac{h_{95}}{k_{95}} \\
  &= \frac{10264770284430115358350493989796951584352149694}{6616509493602288551995313304988866597070326335} \\
  &= 1.5513875245483203922619525102646238151635917038038871995280071201179267425542569572957604536135484903\cdots, \\
\varepsilon &= \frac{1}{k_{95}(k_{95}+k_{94})} \\
            &= 1.82761... \times 10^{-91}.
\end{align}</math>}}

== Base angle and Apex angle ==
The Calabi triangle is [[Obtuse triangle|obtuse]] with base angle {{mvar|θ}} and apex angle {{mvar|ψ}} as follows:
:<math>\begin{align}
\theta &= \cos^{-1}(x/2) \\
       &= 39.13202614232587442003651601935656349795831966723206\cdots^\circ, \\
\psi   &= 180 - 2\theta \\
       &= 101.73594771534825115992696796128687300408336066553587\cdots^\circ. \\
\end{align}</math>
